verses.51:28: Share in instruction for a great sum of silver, and acquire much gold through her.
verses.51:29: May your soul rejoice in His mercy, and may you not be ashamed in His praise.
verses.51:30: Do your work before the time, and He will give your reward in His time."

notes.1:13: The critical Greek text reads 'he will find favor' (εὑρήσει χάριν), whereas some manuscripts read 'he will be blessed.'
notes.1:15: Greek literally reads 'she nested an eternal foundation,' portraying Wisdom making a lasting home among humanity; 'she will be trusted' translates future passive ἐμπιστευθήσεται (also carrying the sense of proving faithful).
notes.1:19: The implied subject of the verbs in this verse is the Lord, echoing 1:9 ('saw and counted her'), while 'her' refers to Wisdom.
notes.1:22: Greek pairs ἄδικος ('unjust') with δικαιωθῆναι ('be justified') in a wordplay; 'weight' renders ῥοπή, literally the downward tipping of a balance scale.
notes.1:29: Greek literally reads 'in the mouths of people' (ἐν στόμασιν ἀνθρώπων), referring to public speech or acting before the scrutiny of others.
notes.2:4: 'Changes' renders ἀλλάγμασιν, referring to shifting circumstances or reversals during humiliation.
notes.2:9: Both 'eternity' and 'mercy' (αἰῶνος καὶ ἐλέους) are Greek genitives modifying 'gladness,' expressing enduring joy grounded in God's mercy.
notes.2:14: 'Visits' renders ἐπισκέπτηται, a biblical idiom for God coming in inspection, reckoning, or judgment.
notes.2:18: Greek uses the future indicative ἐμπεσούμεθα ('We will fall'), expressing firm resolve (often understood cohortatively as 'Let us fall'), echoing 2 Samuel 24:14.
notes.3:5: The Greek text here repeats the clause from v. 4 ("and like one who stores up treasure is the one who glorifies his mother") before concluding with the promise of answered prayer.
notes.3:10: The Greek text reads "with respect to dishonor" (πρὸς ἀτιμίαν); many other Greek witnesses read "a father's dishonor" (πατρὸς ἀτιμία), yielding "for a father's dishonor is not glory to you."
notes.3:14: Greek ἐλεημοσύνη ("mercy," also in v. 30) denotes compassionate aid or charitable kindness; the rare verb προσανοικοδομηθήσεται ("will be built up") carries the sense of being built up additionally or credited to one's account.
notes.3:26: The Greek text places the clause on loving danger first with "will fall into it" (ἐμπεσεῖται, whereas other witnesses read ἀπολεῖται, "will perish"), followed by two parallel clauses on a hard heart (the second echoing v. 27).
notes.4:16: The Greek text shifts abruptly from second person singular ("If you trust, you will inherit her") to third person singular ("his generations"), continuing in third person through vv. 17-19.
notes.4:22: "Show partiality" renders the Greek idiom λάβῃς πρόσωπον (literally "accept a face," also in v. 27), meaning to show deference or favoritism.
notes.4:29: The Greek text reads τραχὺς ("harsh" or "rough"); several other manuscripts read ταχύς ("quick" or "hasty").
notes.4:30: The rare Greek compound φαντασιοκοπῶν ("given to wild fancies") refers to behaving capriciously, wildly, or with paranoid suspicions toward one's household.
notes.5:6: The Greek text reads the genitive par' autou ('from Him'), whereas some manuscripts read the dative par' auto ('with Him'). The verb exilasetai (cognate with exilasmou, 'atonement', in v. 5) carries the sense of atoning for or pardoning sins.
notes.5:8: The Greek text reads the second-person singular opheleseis ('you will gain nothing'), whereas some witnesses read the third-person singular or plural ('it/they will profit nothing').
notes.5:14: The Greek text reads the aorist passive enedreuthes ('do not be entrapped by your tongue'), whereas other witnesses read the active imperative enedreue ('do not lie in wait with your tongue').
notes.6:2: The Saints Greek Critical Text has no verse 6:1; this verse continues the sentence begun in 5:15. It reads the nominative αἰσχύνη ('an evil name is shame, and it will inherit reproach') rather than the accusative αἰσχύνην found in some witnesses.
notes.6:20: The Greek text reads tacheia ('swift', as in major uncials such as Vaticanus), whereas other witnesses and editions read tracheia ('rough/harsh'). The adjective akardios literally means 'without heart', an idiom for lacking sense or understanding.
notes.6:22: The statement that wisdom is 'according to her name' preserves literally a Hebrew wordplay in the underlying text (linking discipline/instruction with what is hidden or turned aside) that does not carry over directly into Greek.
notes.6:29: The Greek text reads kladoi ('branches'), whereas other witnesses read kloioi ('collars', echoing v. 24).
notes.6:37: The Greek text includes the possessive pronoun sou in he epithymia tes sophias sou, translated 'your desire for wisdom' (taking the possessive with the whole phrase, as in Semitic construct idioms); some witnesses omit sou.
notes.7:12: Greek literally reads "plow a lie," reflecting a Hebrew verb (charash) that can mean both "to plow" and "to devise" or "plot."
notes.7:17: In this Greek text, "Remember that wrath will not delay" appears within v. 17 rather than at the end of v. 16 as in some editions; "fire and worm" preserves the Greek singular, echoing Isaiah 66:24.
notes.7:18: "Money" renders Greek adiaphorou (literally "an indifferent thing"), an idiom used in Sirach for financial gain or price; "Souphir" is the Septuagint name corresponding to Hebrew Ophir, renowned for fine gold.
notes.7:31: This Greek text reads ap' arches ("from the beginning"), where some manuscripts read aparchen ("firstfruits") in this position; "the offering for guilt" renders the Septuagint Levitical phrase peri plemmelias.
notes.7:33: The first clause is verbless in Greek (literally "grace of a gift before every living person"); "grace" (charis) here encompasses gracious kindness, including proper care and burial rites for the dead.
notes.8:2: "Overbalance your weight" renders balance-scale imagery in Greek (antistese sou ten holken, literally "weigh against your weight"), pointing to how a wealthy opponent can tip the scales through money.
notes.8:11: "Rise up before" literally translates Greek exanastes, cautioning against being provoked into confronting an insolent person, who waits in ambush to trap one's words.
notes.8:14: Greek doxa here denotes the judge's honor or prestige, though the term can also carry the sense of "opinion" or "judgment."
notes.8:19: The second clause translates the Greek literally ("do not let him return a favor to you"), warning against putting oneself in an untrustworthy person's debt or ironically noting that no kindness will be repaid; the surviving Hebrew text differs here.
notes.9:5: "Her penalties" translates the Greek tois epitimiois autes, referring to the legal fines or penalties incurred for wronging a virgin (cf. Exod 22:16-17; Deut 22:28-29).
notes.9:9: The Greek reads "in your spirit" (to pneumati sou), whereas the surviving Hebrew manuscript tradition reads "in blood," reflecting a textual divergence between the Greek and Hebrew witnesses.
notes.9:14: The verb "assess" renders Greek stochasai (literally "aim at," "gauge," or "estimate"), advising careful discernment of those around one.
notes.10:7: The Greek text given here reads plemmelesi adika ("it will commit unjust things"), a difficult variant alongside plemmeles he adikia ("injustice is offensive") found in some other editions.
notes.10:9: The Greek literally uses the first-person singular erripsa ("I cast out"), either portraying God as speaker or reflecting a difficult Greek rendering of the Hebrew thought that a person's inward parts decay even in life.
notes.10:10: The terse Greek clause makron arrostema, skoptei iatros literally reads "a long illness, a physician mocks" (or "scoffs at"), differing from the Hebrew manuscript tradition, which speaks of a slight illness baffling the physician.
notes.10:20: Verse 10:21 is absent from the main Greek text (appearing only in the expanded Greek tradition), so the verse numbering proceeds directly from 10:20 to 10:22.
notes.10:27: This Greek text reads "works in all things" and "or one who glorifies himself," whereas some other witnesses add "and abounds" before "in all things" and read "and" before "glorifies himself."
notes.11:6: The Greek text reads hetairon ("companions"), whereas other witnesses read the near-homophonous heteron ("others").
notes.11:14: The pair "good and bad" refers here to good fortune and misfortune rather than moral evil. Verses 15-16, found in later expanded Greek manuscripts, are absent from this shorter Greek text.
notes.11:28: The Greek reads "by his children" (en teknois autou), reflecting a rendering of the Hebrew term for "end" or "posterity" as offspring.
notes.11:30: Literally "a hunting partridge in a basket," referring to a caged decoy bird used by fowlers to lure wild partridges into a snare.
notes.12:8: The Greek text reads ekdikethesetai ("will be vindicated"), the reading of the major uncial manuscripts; some modern editors conjecture ekgnosthesetai ("will be known") to align with the Hebrew.
notes.12:11: The Greek clause "it has not corroded to the end" (ouk eis telos katiosen) implies that wiping a bronze mirror never removes its tendency to corrode permanently; the enemy's malice is never finished for good.
notes.13:2: Greek repeats the feminine demonstrative pronoun (haute ... haute), both referring to the fragile clay pot (chytra) rather than the masculine cauldron (lebes).
notes.13:4: Greek ergatai en soi (lit. 'will work in/with you') reflects a Hebrew idiom meaning to put someone to work or exploit their labor.
notes.13:8: The Greek text reads 'in your gladness' (en euphrosyne sou), whereas the Hebrew text reads 'in your folly.'
notes.13:24: The Greek text reads plural 'mouths' (stomasin) and 'a godly person' (eusebous), whereas the Hebrew and some witnesses read 'an ungodly person' (asebous).
notes.14:4: Greek synagon apo tes psyches autou (lit. 'gathering from his own soul') is an idiom for hoarding by depriving or stinting oneself.
notes.14:16: Greek apateson (ordinarily 'deceive' or 'beguile') is used here in its Hellenistic sense of 'indulge,' 'entertain,' or 'treat' oneself.
notes.14:20: The Greek text reads teleutesei ('will die' or 'will end his life'), whereas some Greek witnesses and the Hebrew read 'will meditate' (meletesei).
notes.14:25: Greek kata cheiras autes (lit. 'by her hands') is a Semitic idiom meaning 'beside her' or 'at her side.'
notes.15:2: Literally 'a wife of virginity' (gyne partheneias), rendering the Hebrew idiom for a wife married in youth.
notes.15:11: The Greek text reads second-person singular poieseis ('you must not do' / 'you will not do'), whereas some Greek witnesses and the Hebrew read third-person 'He will not do' (poiesei).
notes.15:14: Greek diaboulion ('deliberation,' 'counsel,' or 'choice') renders the Hebrew term yetser ('inclination' or 'purpose').
notes.15:15: The Greek clause kai pistin poiesai eudokias (lit. 'and to do faithfulness of good pleasure') is terse; the genitive eudokias functions as a predicate genitive indicating that practicing faithfulness is a matter of choice or goodwill.
notes.16:18: The Greek text here includes 'of God' (τοῦ θεοῦ) after 'the heaven of heaven' (as in Codex Vaticanus and Rahlfs), which is omitted in some other Greek witnesses.
notes.16:21: The elliptical Greek opening ('and a tempest that no one will see') differs from the Hebrew of Ben Sira ('if I sin, no eye will see me') and presents God's hidden ways as an unseen storm.
notes.16:26: The Greek text reads 'in the judgment' (ἐν κρίσει), whereas some Greek witnesses read 'in the creation' (ἐν κτίσει), matching the Hebrew ('when God created').
notes.16:27: Greek ἀρχάς can mean either 'dominions' (spheres of rule, as in Genesis 1:16 LXX) or 'beginnings.'
notes.16:30: Literally 'with the soul [or life] of every living creature He covered its face,' using a double accusative construction modeled on the Hebrew idiom.
notes.17:3: The Greek text reads plural καθ᾽ ἑαυτούς ('according to themselves,' as in major uncials B, A, and S), whereas some other witnesses read singular καθ᾽ ἑαυτόν ('like Himself').
notes.17:4: 'The fear of him' (τὸν φόβον αὐτοῦ) refers to the fear of humanity placed upon the creatures (echoing Genesis 9:2), rather than the fear of God.
notes.17:10: Following the order of the Greek text here (as in Codex Vaticanus and Rahlfs), the purpose clause ('so that they might recount...') precedes 'and they will praise the name of holiness'; some editions reverse the two lines.
notes.17:13: The Greek text reads 'their voice' (φωνῆς αὐτῶν, as in Codex Vaticanus), while other Greek witnesses read 'His voice' (φωνῆς αὐτοῦ), referring to God's voice at Sinai.
notes.17:31: The Greek text places 'an evil person' (πονηρός) in the nominative as subject and 'flesh and blood' (σάρκα καὶ αἷμα) in the accusative as object; other witnesses reverse the cases to read 'flesh and blood will ponder evil.'
notes.18:1: Greek koine ('in common' or 'together') likely reflects Hebrew yahdaw ('all alike' or 'without exception'), and was also traditionally understood to mean 'all at once.'
notes.18:9: Greek literally reads 'many, a hundred years' (polla ete hekaton), an idiom meaning 'at most a hundred years' or 'many if they reach a hundred years.'
notes.18:23: Greek euxasthai can mean 'to make a vow' (continuing the subject of v. 22) or 'to pray.'
notes.18:30: 'Self-control of the soul.' is an ancient section heading preserved directly in the Greek manuscript tradition.
notes.18:32: Greek symbolei refers to a 'contribution' or 'share of the expense' (especially for a shared feast; cf. symbolokopon, 'feasting,' in v. 33), though it can also mean 'association.'
notes.19:3: The critical Greek text reads sepe ('decay, rot'), whereas later manuscripts read setes ('moths').
notes.19:5: The critical Greek text reads kardia ('in heart'), while some later manuscripts read kakia ('in wickedness').
notes.19:13: Greek elenxon can mean 'reprove,' 'confront,' or 'question,' alluding to Leviticus 19:17 (cf. v. 17).
notes.19:24: Greek emphobos literally means 'in fear' or 'filled with fear,' referring to the fear of the Lord (v. 20).
notes.19:25: Greek diastrephon charin tou ekphanai krima literally means 'perverting favor to bring forth a judgment,' describing the abuse of favors or kindnesses to obtain a desired legal verdict.
notes.20:8: "Assumes authority for himself" translates the rare Greek compound middle participle ἐνεξουσιαζόμενος, denoting one who arrogates authority to himself.
notes.20:14: Literally "his eyes are many instead of one," a vivid idiom depicting a stingy giver who greedily expects multiple returns for a single gift (cf. v. 15).
notes.20:22: "Because of a senseless person" translates ἀπὸ ἄφρονος προσώπου (literally "from a senseless face/person"), which may refer either to deference to a fool or to foolish concern for appearances.
notes.20:27: "Words of proverbs." renders the Greek section heading Λόγοι παραβολῶν, which is embedded directly in verse 27 in major Septuagint witnesses.
notes.21:5: Neither occurrence of αὐτοῦ has an explicit divine antecedent in Greek; the first ("His ears") refers to God, while the second ("His judgment") may refer either to God's swift judgment or to the poor person's own vindication.
notes.21:8: Greek εἰς χειμῶνα literally reads "for winter" (possibly referring to stockpiling stones uselessly for winter storms, or reflecting an underlying Hebrew wordplay or variant for a burial mound).
notes.21:25: "Will be weighed down" translates βαρυνθήσεται (repeating the verb of v. 24 and contrasting with "weighed on a scale"); some Greek manuscripts instead read διηγήσεται ("will recount").
notes.21:26: The critical Greek text reads the nominative καρδία ("the heart of the wise is their mouth"), whereas some manuscripts read the dative ἐν καρδίᾳ ("in the heart of the wise is their mouth").
notes.21:27: Greek τὸν σατανᾶν (literally "the adversary" or "Satan") transliterates Hebrew שָׂטָן and may refer either to Satan or to a personal adversary.
notes.22:4: Greek kleronomesei ('will inherit') reflects a Semitic idiom for obtaining or winning a husband for herself.
notes.22:6: Greek sophias is genitive ('of wisdom,' i.e., belonging to wisdom); some witnesses read the nominative sophia ('are wisdom').
notes.22:13: Greek entinagmo is a rare noun meaning 'spattering' or 'shaking off,' picturing filth shaken onto a bystander.
notes.22:17: Greek kosmos psammotos (lit. 'sandy ornament') refers to decorative sand-lime plaster or stucco applied to a smoothly dressed wall.
notes.22:27: Greek ap autes ('from it') is feminine singular, referring either to falling away from the guard or seal, or anticipating 'my tongue' ('because of it').
notes.23:2: The Greek shifts from plural pheisontai ('they may not spare,' whips and discipline) to singular pare (from pariemi, 'it will not pass over,' likely the discipline of wisdom) and 'their sins' (auton, referring to his thought and heart, or the lips and tongue of 22:27-23:1).
notes.23:8: Greek kataleiphthesetai literally means 'will be left behind' (or 'abandoned'); many editors regard it as an early spelling variant for katalemphthesetai ('will be caught/overtaken'), paralleling 'be caught' in 23:7.
notes.23:12: Greek antiperibeblemene is a unique compound (lit. 'clothed opposite to'), meaning 'matched with' or 'comparable to' death, pointing to speech such as blasphemy that carries a death-worthy penalty.
notes.23:14: Greek synedreuei is rendered as second person singular ('you sit in council,' as a middle form or variant for synedreueis), and the Greek text retains a resumptive negative me before katarase ('nor curse').
notes.23:16: The phrase 'in the body of his flesh' (en somati sarkos autou) is literal to the Greek and reflects a Semitic idiom that can denote either misuse of one's own physical body or illicit relations with close kin.
notes.24:2: Greek dynameos can mean either "host" (the heavenly army, parallel to "assembly") or "power."
notes.24:6: The Greek text reads ektesamen ("I gained possession"); some commentators emend to hegesamen ("I held sway").
notes.24:14: The Greek text reads en aigialois ("on the shores"), whereas some later manuscripts and versions read the place name "En-gedi."
notes.24:25: The masculine participles in vv. 25-27 resume "the law" (Greek nomos, masculine) from v. 23, though some refer them to God; v. 24 is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts.
notes.24:27: The Greek reads hos phos ("like light"), often thought to reflect Hebrew ke'or ("like light") rather than ki'or ("like the Nile").
notes.25:1: Greek horaia ("beautiful") is feminine singular, probably referring to the speaker's soul (cf. v. 2) or to personified Wisdom from ch. 24.
notes.25:7: Although ten beatitudes are announced, the Greek text lists nine items across vv. 7-10, culminating in the fear of the Lord; v. 12 is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts.
notes.25:15: Greek kephale ("head") renders Hebrew rosh, which means both "head" and "venom/poison."
notes.25:17: The Greek text reads hos sakkon ("like sackcloth"), whereas the Hebrew and some witnesses read "like a bear."
notes.25:18: The Greek text reads akousas ("when he hears"), whereas some manuscripts read akousios ("involuntarily").
notes.26:5: The Greek phrase 'at the fourth face I pleaded' (epi tō tetartō prosōpō edeēthēn) is notoriously difficult; it likely reflects a literal rendering or shift involving 'in the presence of' and 'I feared' or 'I entreated.'
notes.26:10: The Greek text reads the adverb adiatreptōs ('unswervingly'); some manuscripts read the dative adjective adiatreptō ('over a headstrong/shameless daughter').
notes.26:16: The Greek text reads 'his house' (oikias autou, i.e., her husband's house), whereas some manuscripts read 'her house' (autēs).
notes.26:18: The Greek text literally reads 'upon the breast/chest (sternois) of a steadfast woman'; many scholars suspect an early scribal or translational shift from 'heels' (pternais), which would better parallel 'feet' and 'silver base.'
notes.27:1: The Greek text reads adiaphorou ('an indifferent/trifling thing'); some manuscripts read diaphorou ('profit/gain'), which directly continues the commercial theme of 26:29-27:2.
notes.27:2: The Greek verb syntribēsetai normally means 'be crushed' or 'rubbed together,' here used in the sense of being tightly squeezed or wedged in, parallel to the peg between stones.
notes.27:6: The Greek text reads the genitive enthymēmatos ('the speech of the thought of a man's heart'), implying that speech reveals inner cultivation; some manuscripts read the accusative enthymēma ('so does speech reveal the thought of a man's heart').
notes.27:22: The Greek text reads the reflexive hauton ('no one will withdraw himself from him'); reading non-reflexive auton gives 'no one will turn him away from it' (i.e., from evil).
notes.27:23: The Greek text reads 'your mouth' (stoma sou), whereas some manuscripts read 'his mouth' (to stoma autou), matching the second half of the verse.
notes.28:1: The Greek doubles the verb (διαστηριῶν διαστηρίσει, literally 'firmly setting fast, He will set fast'), a Hebraic intensification meaning that the Lord will strictly retain or hold his sins to account, contrasting with 'released' (literally 'loosed') in 28:2.
notes.28:10: The Greek text places the fourth clause ('and according to the strengthening of the strife it will blaze up') at the end of the verse, whereas some manuscripts and editions transpose it directly after the first clause.
notes.28:14: 'A third tongue' (γλῶσσα τρίτη) is a Semitic idiom for a slanderer or gossip whose words enter as a third party to divide two others.
notes.28:18: 'By the edge of the sword' renders the literal Greek idiom 'by the mouth of the sword' (ἐν στόματι μαχαίρας), forming a wordplay with 'the tongue' in the second clause.
notes.29:6: The primary Greek uncial text reads 'not for nothing' (οὐ δωρεάν), emphasizing ironically that the lender paid for an enemy with his lost loan; some witnesses omit 'not' and read 'for nothing' (without cause).
notes.29:8: The Greek text here lacks a negative particle and uses the future indicative ('you will delay him for almsgiving'); several later manuscripts and versions read a negative prohibition ('do not keep him waiting for almsgiving').
notes.29:23: The primary Greek uncials preserve only this single clause; some manuscripts and versions add a second clause ('and you will not hear the reproach of your sojourning').
notes.29:27: 'From the presence of honor' (ἀπὸ προσώπου δόξης) is a Semitic idiom meaning to yield one's place to a more honored person.
notes.30:1: The Greek manuscript text includes the section heading 'Concerning children' at the start of the verse.
notes.30:4: The Greek text reads accented 'kai hos' ('and even so'); some editions accent it as 'hos' ('as though he did not die').
notes.30:7: The Greek text reads 'peri psychon huion' ('for the souls of sons'), reflecting an ancient word-division difference from 'peripsychon huion' ('pampering a son').
notes.30:13: The Greek text reads 'in your disgrace he may stumble'; other textual witnesses read 'at his shameful conduct you may stumble.'
notes.30:25: Greek 'lampra kardia' ('a bright heart') denotes a cheerful or generous disposition, and 'epimelesetai' ('will attend to') conveys caring for or enjoying its food. From here through 36:16 the English keeps the Saints.Bible verse slots shared with the Latin edition (the restored chapter order); the Saints Greek Critical Text follows the manuscript order (Swete), so its verse numbers differ throughout this section.
notes.31:2: The Greek text reads 'apaitesei' ('will demand [slumber]'), whereas other witnesses read a verb meaning 'drives away'; 'eknepsei' literally means 'will sober away' or 'dispel.'
notes.31:5: The Greek text reads 'diaphthoran' ('corruption') and nominative 'autos plesthesetai' ('he himself will be filled'), while other witnesses read 'will be filled with it' or 'will be led astray.'
notes.31:13: 'An evil eye' is an idiom for greed or stinginess; 'from every face' literally renders a Hebrew idiom meaning 'at everything' or 'in every direction.'
notes.31:21: Greek 'mesoporon' literally means 'going midway,' an expression for excusing oneself in the middle of a banquet to find relief from overeating.
notes.31:24: Greek 'poneros' and 'poneria' (literally 'evil') carry the idiomatic sense of 'stingy' and 'stinginess' when used in connection with sharing bread.
notes.32:7: The Greek word order literally reads 'scarcely twice if you are asked,' which can mean speaking at most twice when questioned or speaking reluctantly even if asked twice.
notes.32:14: Greek paidian here is a manuscript spelling variant of paideian ('discipline' or 'instruction'). 'Those who rise early' is a Septuagint idiom for seeking the Lord diligently.
notes.32:17: Greek synkrima means a comparison, interpretation, or ruling, here referring to a precedent or pretext suited to the sinner's own will.
notes.32:18: The Greek text reads allotrios ('stranger' or 'outsider') and ends with an obscure clause literally meaning 'even after acting with him/himself without counsel,' where autou is taken reflexively (compare 33:12).
notes.33:1: Greek exeleitai is a middle form that can be read passively ('he will be delivered') or actively with the Lord as implied subject ('He will deliver him').
notes.33:3: The Greek text here reads dikaion ('of the righteous'), whereas some editions adopt the reading delon ('of the Urim').
notes.33:17: This critical text does not include the line numbered 33:16 in some editions ('I was the last to keep watch'), so 33:17 opens directly with the participial comparison.
notes.33:31: Greek en haimati ('with blood') literally renders a Hebrew idiom for 'with money' or 'at a price,' while in Greek also conveying a costly acquisition.
notes.33:32: This critical text reads the noun epideesis with the dative auto ('there is need for him'), whereas many other witnesses read the verb epideeseis autou ('you will have need of him').
notes.34:3: Literally "this opposite that," comparing a dream to an insubstantial mirror reflection of a face opposite a face.
notes.34:9: The Greek text reads "instructed" (πεπαιδευμένος), whereas some witnesses read "traveled" (πεπλανημένος), matching the vocabulary of vv. 10-11.
notes.34:10: Greek πεπλανημένος (and ἀποπλάνησις in v. 11) literally denotes wandering or roaming, used here in the positive sense of traveling widely abroad.
notes.34:18: The Greek text reads μεμωκημένη and μωκήματα ("mocked" and "mockeries," from μωκάομαι), while some manuscripts read μεμωμημένη and μωμήματα ("blemished" and "blemishes").
notes.35:1: "Deliverance offering" translates Greek σωτηρίου, the standard Septuagint term for the Old Testament peace or fellowship offering.
notes.35:7: Literally "with a good eye" (repeated in v. 9), a Hebrew idiom denoting generosity and a willing spirit.
notes.35:12: "Partiality" translates Greek δόξα προσώπου, literally "glory of a face," meaning favoritism based on outward status or appearance.
notes.35:24: Greek αὐτοῦ ("his") is masculine singular, referring either to an afflicted person or back to the singular noun "people" (λαός) in v. 22.
notes.36:5: Greek ἀλλοίωσον literally means "make other" or "make different," reflecting a Hebrew verb (shanah) that can mean either "change" or "repeat."
notes.36:10: The clause "And I was the last to keep watch" (Κἀγὼ ἔσχατος ἠγρύπνησα) is a textual dislocation from Sirach 33:16 preserved at the seam of transposed leaves in Greek manuscripts. Also, κατακληρονομήσεις αὐτούς ("give them an inheritance") can alternatively mean "take them as Your inheritance."
notes.36:13: "Proclamation of Your wonders" renders the rare Greek term ἀρεταλογία (recounting of divine mighty deeds). The Greek text reads "Your people" (τὸν λαόν σου), whereas some witnesses read "Your temple" (τὸν ναόν σου).
notes.36:23: Literally "not according to the sons of men," an idiom meaning that her husband is uniquely fortunate beyond ordinary mortals.
notes.36:26: The Greek text reads σφαλλομένῳ (literally "stumbling" or "straying"), whereas some witnesses and emendations read ἀφαλλομένῳ ("leaping" or "darting").
notes.37:6: The Greek text reads "in your soul," whereas some witnesses and the Hebrew read "in battle" (reflecting two readings of the underlying Hebrew term).
notes.37:11: The Greek omits the preposition "concerning" before "her rival," using a bare genitive of reference. "Nonresident hired worker" renders Greek misthiou aphestiou ("away from the hearth/home"), where other manuscripts read epeteiou ("yearly").
notes.37:14: The Greek omits an explicit comparative adverb ("better" or "more") before "than," forming an elliptical comparative idiom.
notes.37:17: The Greek critical text prints the dative kardia ("in the heart"), yielding "A trace of change is in the heart," while some editions accent it as nominative ("the heart is the trace of change").
notes.37:30: Greek cholera here denotes a violent bilious illness or colic rather than modern Asiatic cholera.
notes.38:7: The Greek leaves the subject of "heals" unexpressed (implicitly the physician, or possibly the Lord from v. 6), with "his pain" referring to the sufferer's pain. In v. 8, ou me syntelese erga autou may also be taken intransitively as "His works will never come to an end."
notes.38:11: Literally "as one who does not exist" (hos me hyparchon), perhaps understood as "as if near death" or "sparing nothing"; the extant Hebrew differs, reading "according to your means."
notes.38:19: A notoriously difficult Greek line: apagoge literally means "carrying off" (calamity or bereavement), and parabainei means "passes by" (other manuscripts read paramenei, "remains"). "Against the heart" (kata kardias) conveys a burden or affliction to the heart.
notes.38:28: The critical text reads "unworked iron" (argo sidero, vs. variant "work of iron"), "will harden" (pexei, vs. variant "will melt"), and "will renew his ear" (kainiei, ringing afresh in his ear, where some scholars conjecture a textual error for "deafens" or "inclines").
notes.38:30: "Its strength" (ischyn autou) refers to the stiffness of the masculine noun "clay" (or possibly "his own strength"). "The gift" translates the manuscript reading to charisma, which many editors emend to to chrisma ("the glaze").
notes.38:34: Following the traditional Greek versification, the final clause of 38:34 opens the sentence that continues directly into 39:1.
notes.39:7: The pronouns are grammatically ambiguous; "His hidden things" refers to the mysteries of the Lord (v. 6), while "He himself" and "his counsel" refer to the scribe.
notes.39:11: The Greek comparative "than a thousand" omits "greater," and the verb rendered "suffices for him" means "is enough for him" or "works to his advantage."
notes.39:26: This Greek text reads nominative "wheat" as a separate item after "fine flour," rather than genitive "of wheat" as in some witnesses.
notes.39:28: Or "winds"; Greek pneumata can denote either destructive spirits or storm winds.
notes.39:35: This Greek text reads the first-person plural indicative "we have sung praise," whereas some manuscripts read the second-person plural imperative "sing praise."
notes.40:1: This Greek text reads "for burial" (epi taphe), whereas some other witnesses read "of return" (epistrophes).
notes.40:9: This Greek text ends after "sword," without the additional list of calamities found in some other witnesses.
notes.40:14: The obscure Greek phrase "when he opens his hands" likely arose from a Greek rendering of a Hebrew image about a torrent lifting rocks, reading the Hebrew word for "rocks" as "hands."
notes.40:18: This Greek text lacks "and" between "self-sufficient" and "laborer," even though the second clause refers to "both."
notes.40:25: This Greek text reads "a wife" (gyne), whereas other witnesses read "counsel" (boule).
notes.40:27: This Greek text reads third-person plural "they have covered it," an impersonal plural or variant for singular "it covers" found in some other witnesses.
notes.41:2: Greek apeithounti literally means 'disobedient' or 'refusing to comply,' conveying a person stubbornly or despairingly at odds with life.
notes.41:4: Greek elegmos zoes literally means 'reproof' or 'inquiry of life,' expressing that in Hades there is no questioning or argument over the length of one's life.
notes.41:19: The Greek literally reads 'and before the truth of God and the covenant' without naming a separate offense, either continuing from the preceding clause or reflecting an ancient translation rendering of a Hebrew clause about breaking an oath and covenant.
notes.41:23: The Saints Greek Critical Text gives this line twice: here, and again at the opening of 41:24; both are translated as they stand.
notes.42:2: Greek dikaiosai ton asebe literally means 'to acquit the ungodly'; in context it either connects back to 'do not show partiality so as to sin' (42:1) or refers to judging impartially even when the verdict favors an ungodly person in a particular dispute.
notes.42:5: Greek adiaphorou (lit. 'indifferent' or 'an indifferent thing') is used in Sirach (cf. 7:18) for impartial dealing or monetary price/gain in trade, closely related to diaphoron ('price, profit').
notes.42:18: The Greek text reads the first-person dienoethen ('I have reflected on'), a well-attested early manuscript reading alongside the third-person dienoethe ('He reflected on/understood') in other witnesses.
notes.42:21: The Greek text reads kai heos estin ('and as long as He exists'), a manuscript reading corresponding to hos estin ('as He is') in other Greek witnesses.
notes.42:22: The Greek phrase hos spintheros estin theoresai (lit. 'as of a spark it is to look upon') is difficult; the genitive spintheros may express that human observation catches only a spark-like glimpse of God's works or may reflect heos ('even down to a spark').
notes.43:8: The Greek text reads "a vessel of parables" (skeuos parabolon), following major uncial manuscripts, whereas other Greek witnesses read "of the armies" or "encampments" (parembolon).
notes.43:9: The Greek text reads "the Lord" in the nominative case (Kyrios), yielding "in the highest places is the Lord," whereas some manuscripts read the genitive (Kyriou), "in the heights of the Lord."
notes.43:17: The Greek text reads "reproached" (oneidisen), whereas some critical editions adopt the variant "made writhe in labor" (odinesen).
notes.43:23: The Greek text literally reads "and Jesus planted it" (ephyteusen auten Iesous), a well-known reading of major Septuagint manuscripts arising from an early scribal misreading of "planted islands in it" (en aute nesous).
notes.43:26: The Greek text reads "a sweet aroma is His end" (euodia telos autou), matching major uncial manuscripts, whereas other witnesses read "His messenger prospers" (euodoi angelos autou).
notes.44:3: The Greek text uses the future indicative "they will take counsel" (bouleusontai), whereas other witnesses read a participle ("giving counsel").
notes.44:4: The Greek text reads the genitive noun "of learning" (grammateias), whereas some manuscripts read the plural noun "scribes" (grammateis).
notes.44:11: The phrase "In the covenants" stands at the end of verse 11 in the Greek text and completes its clause at the start of verse 12.
notes.44:17: The Greek text repeats "therefore" (dia touto) before "a flood came," whereas other witnesses read "when" (hote); "replacement" translates antallagma (literally "exchange" or "substitute").
notes.45:3: Greek κατέπαυσεν literally means "caused to cease" (recalling Moses stopping the plagues at his word), whereas the surviving Hebrew manuscript reads "hastened"; τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ is a partitive genitive ("part of His glory").
notes.45:10: "Oracle of judgment" (λογίῳ κρίσεως) and "manifestations of truth" (δήλοις ἀληθείας) are the Septuagint terms corresponding to the high priest's breastpiece and the Urim (cf. Exod 28:30).
notes.45:12: The neuter plural adjective ὡραῖα ("Beautiful things") stands at the end of verse 12 in this versification and introduces the clause completed in verse 13.
notes.45:17: The critical text reads φωνῆσαι ("to call/summon"), whereas other manuscripts read φωτίσαι ("to enlighten").
notes.45:25: The critical text omits "Jesse" after υἱῷ ("a son") and contrasts Davidic royal succession (passing to one son from a son) with Aaron's priestly inheritance shared across his seed.
notes.46:1: Greek Ἰησοῦς Ναυῆ ("Joshua son of Nun") creates a wordplay between Joshua's name ("the Lord saves") and "salvation" (σωτηρίᾳ).
notes.46:3: The critical text reads τοὺς γὰρ πολεμίους Κύριος αὐτὸς ἐπήγαγεν ("for the Lord Himself brought on the enemies"), whereas other witnesses read "for he himself waged the wars of the Lord."
notes.46:7: Greek reads ἐχθροῦ ("an enemy"), whereas the surviving Hebrew text reads "the assembly/congregation" (alluding to Num 14:6-10).
notes.46:13: The critical text omits the proper name "Samuel" (present in other witnesses), identifying him only by title, and reads βασιλέα ("a king") rather than βασιλείαν ("a kingdom").
notes.46:18: Greek reads Τυρίων ("of the Tyrians"), reflecting a rendering of the Hebrew word for "enemy/foe" as the city name Tyre.
notes.47:5: The critical text omits δυνατόν ("mighty") after ἄνθρωπον ("a man") and reads the future indicative ἀνυψώσει ("He will lift up") where other witnesses read the infinitive ἀνυψῶσαι ("to lift up").
notes.47:6: The critical text has singular verbs ἐδόξασεν and ᾔνεσεν ("He glorified... praised"), whereas other witnesses read plural ("they glorified... praised," echoing 1 Sam 18:7).
notes.47:20: The critical text reads the first-person singular κατενύγην ("I was grieved"), where other manuscripts read the infinitive κατανυγῆναι ("so that grief came").
notes.47:22: Greek reads ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ ("of His works"), whereas the surviving Hebrew manuscript reads "of His words."
notes.48:11: This Greek text reads 'adorned' (κεκοσμημένοι), whereas some witnesses read 'fallen asleep' (κεκοιμημένοι). 'Will surely live' renders a Hebraic emphatic idiom literally meaning 'will live with life.'
notes.48:17: The Greek text reads the proper name 'Gog' (τὸν Γώγ), widely understood as an ancient scribal corruption for the spring 'Gihon' (cf. 2 Chr 32:30), whose waters Hezekiah channeled into Jerusalem.
notes.48:18: The Greek text places 'his hand' in the nominative case as subject ('his hand rose up'), whereas some manuscripts read the accusative ('he lifted up his hand').
notes.49:9: The Greek syntax is difficult, joining an infinitive ('to do good') to 'remembered,' and diverges sharply from the Hebrew Ben Sira manuscript, which states that Ezekiel made mention of Job.
notes.49:10: This Greek text reads singular verbs ('He comforted... redeemed'), likely referring to God (cf. 48:20), whereas other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew read plural verbs referring to the twelve prophets.
notes.49:12: This Greek text reads 'a holy people' (λαὸν ἅγιον), whereas other witnesses and the Hebrew read 'a holy temple' (ναὸν ἅγιον).
notes.49:13: This Greek text reads the verb 'they maintain' (νέμουσιν) where other Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew read the proper name 'Nehemiah' (Νεεμίου).
notes.49:15: This Greek text reads 'And Joseph' (ὁ δὲ Ἰωσήφ), whereas other Greek witnesses read 'Neither was a man born like Joseph' (οὐδὲ ὡς Ἰωσήφ).
notes.50:3: The Greek verb literally means 'was diminished' (ἠλαττώθη), where the Hebrew reads 'was dug,' and 'bronze' (χαλκός) alludes to Solomon's bronze sea (1 Kgs 7:23).
notes.50:12: This Greek text reads the nominative 'he himself' (αὐτός), whereas other witnesses read the genitive 'around him' (αὐτοῦ).
notes.50:18: This Greek text reads 'in the vast house' (ἐν πλείστῳ οἴκῳ, the reading of the major Greek uncials), which some editors emend to 'with the greatest sound' (ἐν πλείστῳ ἤχῳ).
notes.50:20: This Greek text reads the dative 'to the Lord' (Κυρίῳ), whereas other manuscripts read the genitive 'of the Lord' (Κυρίου), referring to the priestly blessing.
notes.50:21: This Greek text reads singular 'he bowed a second time' (ἐδευτέρωσεν) and 'to show forth' (ἐπιδείξασθαι), whereas other witnesses read plural 'they bowed a second time' (ἐδευτέρωσαν) and 'to receive' (ἐπιδέξασθαι).
notes.50:26: The Greek text reads 'Mount Samaria' (ὄρει Σαμαρείας), whereas the Hebrew Ben Sira manuscript reads 'Mount Seir' (Edom).
notes.51:3: The Greek literally has the nominative singular ἕτοιμος εἰς βρῶμα ("ready for food"), which may refer either to the speaker as ready to become prey or, by grammatical discord (where other witnesses read the genitive plural ἑτοίμων), to gnashing jaws ready to devour.
notes.51:6: The verbless opening phrase ("To a king, the slander of an unrighteous tongue") is sometimes joined to the end of verse 5. The verb "praised" translates the Greek reading ᾔνεσεν found in major uncial witnesses, whereas other manuscripts and the Hebrew parallel reflect ἤγγισεν ("drew near").
notes.51:10: The Greek phrase 'the Lord, the Father of my lord' is an unusual address whose wording is debated.
notes.51:19: "In the practice of hunger" translates the Greek reading λιμοῦ ("hunger/famine") found in early uncial manuscripts, whereas other Greek witnesses read νόμου ("of the law").
notes.51:20: The Greek text places this clause before "and in purification I found her" and reads the plural pronoun μετ᾽ αὐτῶν ("with them"), whereas other witnesses invert the clauses and read the singular μετ᾽ αὐτῆς ("with her").

unplaced.text: Since many great things have been given to us through the Law and the Prophets and the others who followed after them—for which Israel ought to be praised for instruction and wisdom, and since not only ought the readers themselves to become knowledgeable, but lovers of learning should also be able to be useful to outsiders both in speaking and in writing—my grandfather Jesus, after devoting himself extensively to the reading of the Law and the Prophets and the other ancestral books, and having acquired considerable proficiency in them, was himself also led to compose something pertaining to instruction and wisdom, so that lovers of learning, becoming committed to these writings as well, might make much greater progress in living according to the Law. You are urged, therefore, to read with goodwill and attention, and to show forbearance wherever we may seem to fall short in some of the expressions we have labored over in translation; for things spoken in Hebrew do not have the same force in themselves as when they are carried over into another language. And not only these, but the Law itself, and the prophecies, and the rest of the books have no small difference when spoken in their original language. For when I arrived in Egypt in the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes and stayed for a time, I found a copy of no small instruction; I judged it most necessary myself to apply some diligence and labor to translating this book. Indeed, I have devoted much sleepless effort and skill over that span of time to bringing the book to completion and publishing it also for those living abroad who wish to love learning, preparing their character to live according to the Law.
unplaced.note: The Greek translator's prologue by the grandson of Jesus ben Sira, dated to the thirty-eighth year of Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II (132 BC), is the earliest witness to the threefold division of Israel's Scriptures ('the Law and the Prophets and the other ancestral books') and reflects on the inherent challenges of translating Hebrew into Greek.
